item.mechanism: Micro-galvanic coupling between dual phases drives selective dissolution of the less noble BCC phase, acting as the anode, while the nobler FCC phase acts as the cathode.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA and DS2205 duplex steel
item.supporting_observation: Selective dissolution of the B2 phase in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205 was observed via SEM, correlated with Volta potential differences measured by SKP.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is specific to dual-phase alloys with a significant Volta potential difference (~50 mV for EHEA, ~35 mV for DS2205); the text notes that the degree of coupling depends on phase volume fraction and chemistry.
item.alternatives_considered: Uniform corrosion without phase selectivity; the text explicitly contrasts the observed selective dissolution with uniform pitting.
quotes: This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
Selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205.
The overall relative work function potential of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy (average ~50 mV) was higher compared to DS2205 alloy (average ~−65 mV), indicating the nobility of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 versus DS2205.

item.mechanism: Aluminum acts as a sacrificial element forming a redox buffer (Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2) that thermodynamically suppresses the dissolution of noble elements (Co, Ni, Fe).
item.supporting_observation: Enrichment of Co and Ni in the near-surface region and reduced Cr depletion depth (~50 μm) compared to DS2205 (~300 μm) at 650 °C.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism relies on the presence of Al; the text states this effect was not observed in DS2205 due to the lack of a stable Al/AlCl3 redox couple.
item.alternatives_considered: Direct dissolution of Cr and Fe without redox buffering; the text attributes the lower corrosion rate of EHEA specifically to the Al sacrificial effect.
quotes: This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205.
These findings suggest that Al/AlCl 3 and Cr/CrCl 2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi 2.1.
Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl 3 and CrCl 2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl 3 and Cr/CrCl 2 .

item.mechanism: The FCC-L1 2 phase acts as a barrier against further oxidation, protecting the underlying BCC-B2 phase through the enrichment of noble elements in the surface layer.
item.supporting_observation: Work function increased with temperature, and EDS maps showed enrichment of Co and Ni in the corrosion layer while Al and Cr were depleted.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that at 650 °C, uniform pitting was observed on the EHEA surface, suggesting the barrier effect may be overwhelmed or altered at higher temperatures compared to 450 °C.
item.alternatives_considered: The text contrasts this with DS2205 where such enrichment and barrier formation did not occur to the same extent.
quotes: Additionally, the work function increased with increasing temperature for AlCoCrFeNi 2.1, indicating that the FCC-L1 2 phase acted as a barrier against further oxidation and protected the underlying BCC-B2 phase with enrichment of noble elements in the protective surface layer.
Figure 6 a,c shows that there is enrichment of Co and Ni (and to some degree Fe) in the near-surface region even more than the bulk alloy.

item.mechanism: Thermodynamic driving force based on Gibbs free energy of chloride formation dictates the order of element depletion (dealloying), with elements forming chlorides of lower ΔG° reacting preferentially.
item.supporting_observation: FactSage calculations predicted Al > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni reactivity for EHEA and Si > Mn > Cr > Fe > Ni > Mo for DS2205, matching observed depletion patterns.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism assumes thermodynamic control; the text mentions that kinetic factors and impurities also play a role, and that trace impurities may contribute to relative dissolution rates.
item.alternatives_considered: Kinetic control solely; the authors explicitly use thermodynamic calculations to explain the preferential leaching order.
quotes: This leads to thermodynamic driving force for selective depletion of the alloying elements, i.e., dealloying at the surface.

item.mechanism: Impurity metal chlorides (Ni2+, Fe2+, Co2+) in the salt react with the alloy, causing reduction of ions to atomic form and enrichment in the corrosion layer, enhancing resistance.
item.supporting_observation: Enrichment of Co, Ni, and Fe in the near-surface region was observed, which the authors attribute to the reduction of impurity ions at the surface.
item.scope_limits: The text states this effect was not observed in DS2205, likely due to the lack of the stable Al/AlCl3 redox couple that facilitates this process.
item.alternatives_considered: Direct dissolution of alloy elements without impurity interaction; the authors propose the impurity reaction as a specific mitigation mechanism for EHEA.
quotes: Metallic chloride impurities (e.g., NiCl 2 , FeCl 2 , CoCl 2 ), commonly present in NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 molten salt, may react with the alloying elements, leading to their dissolution in the melt.
Ni 2+ , Co 2+ , and Fe 2+ ions were reduced to atomic Ni, Co, and Fe at the surface and their diffusion was likely assisted by vacancies created during depletion of Al and Cr.

Metallic impurities such as Ni 2+ , Fe 2+ , and Co 2+ enhance the corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 via enrichment of impurity ions such as Ni, Co, and Fe (to lesser extent) in the corrosion layer as temperature increases.

item.mechanism: Moisture and oxide impurities in the salt react with refractory elements like Molybdenum to form unstable or volatile oxides, causing Mo depletion.
item.supporting_observation: Significant depletion of Mo was observed in DS2205 despite thermodynamic calculations suggesting MoCl2 formation is unfavorable (high ΔG°).
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is specific to DS2205 and the presence of moisture/oxide impurities; it does not apply to AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 where Mo is not a primary constituent.
item.alternatives_considered: Chloride formation as the cause of Mo loss; the text explicitly rules this out due to high ΔG° for MoCl2.
quotes: Hence, depletion of Mo in DS2205 may be caused by direct reaction with moisture and oxide impurities, resulting in the formation of unstable or volatile metallic oxides as follows.
Figure 7 shows relatively high ΔG° for MoCl 2 , so depletion of Mo due to chloride formation is not expected.

item.mechanism: Higher volume fraction of the anodic BCC phase increases susceptibility to galvanic corrosion; a lower volume fraction makes the alloy less prone to this mechanism.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA (23% BCC) vs DS2205 (higher BCC fraction)
item.supporting_observation: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 has ~23% BCC phase while DS2205 has a higher fraction, correlating with the lower corrosion rate and less severe selective dissolution in EHEA.
item.scope_limits: This is a comparative observation; the text does not provide a quantitative threshold where the mechanism fails, but notes the degree of coupling depends on volume fraction.
item.alternatives_considered: The text considers phase chemistry and Volta potential as primary drivers, with volume fraction acting as a modifier of the galvanic severity.
quotes: A lower volume fraction of the BCC phase, which makes it less prone to galvanic corrosion.
Previous studies suggest that the relative chemistry difference and phase volume fraction (FCC:BCC) determine the degree of degree of galvanic coupling in dual-phase alloys.
The EBSD phase map in Figure 2 b shows the lamellar structure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 with FCC (red color ~77%) and BCC (green color ~23%) phases.

item.mechanism: Increased temperature destabilizes the surface oxide layer, leading to unstable growth initially and higher corrosion rates due to increased dissolution kinetics.
item.supporting_observation: OCP showed poor stability for the first 30 min at 650 °C compared to 450 °C; corrosion rates increased significantly with temperature for both alloys.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that despite the initial instability at 650 °C, the EHEA still maintained superior resistance compared to DS2205 at both temperatures.
item.alternatives_considered: Stable passivation at all temperatures; the authors explicitly state that the increase in temperature resulted in unstable growth of surface oxide initially.
quotes: At 650 °C, both the alloys showed relatively poor stability for the first 30 min, suggesting that an increase in temperature might have resulted in the unstable growth of surface oxide initially, before reaching steady state.
The I corr value increased with an increase in temperature for both alloys, indicating the high dissolution rate and relatively poor protective nature of their surface passivation layer.
Greater material loss was observed with an increase in temperature, which supports the potentiodynamic study.
